content: Corticosteroid therapy is a cornerstone in the management of nephrotic syndrome in children, a condition characterized by protein leakage from the blood into the urine through the glomeruli, leading to hypoproteinemia and generalized edema. While the majority of children with nephrotic syndrome respond to corticosteroid treatment, approximately 80% experience a relapsing course. The introduction of corticosteroids has significantly reduced the mortality rate associated with nephrotic syndrome to around 3%. However, corticosteroids are associated with well-documented adverse effects, including obesity, impaired growth, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and behavioral disturbances. This review, updated in 2020, aimed to evaluate the benefits and harms of various corticosteroid regimens in children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS). The analysis focused on two groups: children experiencing their initial episode of SSNS and those with a relapsing course of the disease. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different durations, total doses, or dosing strategies of corticosteroid therapy in children aged 1 to 18 years. The review identified 48 studies involving 3,941 participants, with 16 new studies added since the last update. However, the methodological quality of many studies was suboptimal. Only 25 studies demonstrated low risk of bias for random sequence generation, and 22 studies for allocation concealment. Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) was adequately addressed in only 9 studies, while outcome assessment (detection bias) was blinded in 11 studies, 9 of which were placebo-controlled RCTs. Fewer than half of the studies were at low risk for attrition bias (22 studies) and reporting bias (23 studies). In children with their initial episode of SSNS, seven studies with low risk of selection bias showed no significant difference in the frequency of relapses when comparing two months of prednisone therapy to three months or longer (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.19; 585 participants; 4 studies; I² = 0%) or three months to five to seven months of therapy (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.33; 376 participants; 3 studies; I² = 35%). Similarly, eight studies found no significant difference in the number of children experiencing any relapse within 12 to 24 months when comparing two months of prednisone to three months or longer (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.06; 637 participants; 5 studies; I² = 47%) or three months to five to seven months of therapy (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.11; 377 participants; 3 studies; I² = 53%). Adverse effects were comparable across different treatment durations. In children with relapsing SSNS, two small studies found no difference in the time to remission between a prednisone dose of 1 mg/kg and the conventional dose of 2 mg/kg (MD 0.71 days, 95% CI -0.43 to 1.86; 79 participants). However, the total prednisone dose was lower with the reduced dosing regimen (MD -20.60 mg/kg, 95% CI -25.65 to -15.55; 20 participants). Two studies comparing dosing by weight versus dosing by surface area found no significant difference in relapse rates at six months (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.49; 146 participants). One study reported a reduced risk of relapse with daily low-dose prednisone compared to alternate-day dosing (MD -0.90 relapses/year, 95% CI -1.33 to -0.47). Additionally, four studies demonstrated that daily prednisone during viral infections reduced the risk of relapse compared to alternate-day prednisone or no treatment. The authors concluded that four well-designed studies involving 823 children have established that extending prednisone therapy beyond two to three months in the first episode of SSNS offers no additional benefit. Small studies in children with relapsing disease suggest no difference in remission times when using half the conventional induction dose of 2 mg/kg or 60 mg/m². Larger studies are needed to confirm these findings. Furthermore, daily low-dose prednisone during intercurrent infections appears to reduce the risk of relapse compared to alternate-day or no prednisone therapy. Results from a larger RCT involving over 300 children are awaited to better understand the relative efficacy and adverse effects of alternate-day versus daily prednisone in preventing relapses during infections.
